analysis.title: 72% Of The Tokens, 27% Of The Money: The AI Demand Data Both Bulls And Bears Are Using To Prove They're Right
key_insights: Goldman's Bobby Molavi says AI demand data supports both bulls and bears. His view is that 'one thing is clear for now...the demand is growing', and what that demand is worth is the open question.

Token demand is up 27x since last November per OpenRouter, with open-weight models at 72% of those tokens. OpenRouter weekly volume went from 0.5 trillion tokens in mid-January 2025 to 128.4 trillion in the week of September 14, roughly 250x in 20 months.

GPU rental pricing is rising: H200 up 160% YTD, B200 up 120%, H100 up 35%. Even the 6-year-old A100 rents for more than at the start of the year, which bears on GPU depreciation schedules and hyperscaler earnings.

The GPU useful-life accounting dispute: if a GPU is economically dead after three years, hyperscaler earnings are flattered by six-year depreciation schedules. A 2020-vintage A100 earning more than in January is cited as the bulls' best evidence that chips last longer than skeptics assumed.

Epoch AI (Sep 22) finds the price of reaching a given AI performance level has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, roughly 13x per year, and about 66% per quarter (75x per year) near the frontier.
Epoch example: in January 2025 OpenAI's o3 cost about $0.30 per question to score 75% on GPQA Diamond. GPT-5.6 Luna hits the same score for $0.0004 per question, a 725-fold drop in under 18 months.
LLM inference prices have fallen 4x faster than DNA sequencing, 6x faster than computing power (1940-2001), 18x faster than lithium-ion batteries and 54x faster than electricity, per Epoch.

What customers pay falls more slowly than list price because they trade up. YipitData found effective API token pricing fell 39% in 2H25 (44% on OpenRouter) but only 6% YTD through May 2026. OpenRouter blended pricing fell about 15% in Q1, and enterprises are raising the share of tokens going to high-end models.

OpenRouter data: open-weight models handled 72% of tokens but collected 27% of spend in the second week of September. Closed-weight models took 73% of spend, down from 89% in the first week of January. 69% of OpenRouter tokens in mid-September came from Chinese labs.

Rising GPU rents and falling token prices are described as the same squeeze from two ends: serving cost per token is rising while the selling price falls. This favors GPU lessors over the companies paying the rents.

A strategist report cited by Molavi finds AI not yet showing productivity gains outside tech: revenue per worker and profit margins are up for the Mag 7 but flat for the S&P 493. Corporate buyers are shifting from token spend tied to growth toward token spend, costs and margin impact.

Molavi describes an AI capex 'boom loop': hyperscaler spend drives ecosystem revenue, which pulls in venture and growth capital. The risk is whether those revenues persist without the capex anchor. Vendor financing ('balance sheet as a service') blurs revenue and financing lines.

Private-market AI exits are described as spectacular but highly concentrated and interdependent (SpaceX, Cerebras, Cursor, Hugging Face), with some valuation ramps having 'no catalyst to the rerate other than a termsheet'.

Meta tapped shareholders for up to $95 billion with its chip suppliers buying in, with the debt window described as shut. ZeroHedge calls this vendor financing in equity form and says it expects the bears to win the debate.

sector_views.rationale: Demand is growing but value capture is contested. Revenue accrues to cheaper open-weight models and GPU owners, while payers of GPU rents face margin pressure. Goldman's Molavi frames it as a bull-bear tug of war. The ZeroHedge author leans bearish.

risk_factors: Token price deflation outpaces volume growth in revenue terms, so cost per token versus revenue per token moves the wrong way as power shifts to open-weight models.
AI revenue sustainability without the hyperscaler capex anchor is unproven.
Vendor financing and equity raises blur revenue and financing lines.
Concentrated, interdependent private-market exits and valuations with no catalyst other than a termsheet.
Benefits are not yet visible in the S&P 493's revenue per worker or margins.
The enterprise shift toward measuring token spend against margins and costs.

tension_points.bull_case: Token demand is up 27x since last November and about 250x in 20 months. GPU rents are rising across A100, H100, H200 and B200, which supports longer chip useful lives and broader demand and TAM growth.
tension_points.bear_case: Open-weight models carry 72% of tokens but 27% of spend. Cost per token versus revenue per token is moving the wrong way, and the S&P 493 shows no productivity or margin gains.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Closed-weight spend share keeps falling from 89% in January toward the 73% seen in September, or revenue persists without the hyperscaler capex anchor.

theme_stances.key_argument: Most volume growth flows to the models that charge the least, while GPU serving costs rise.
theme_stances.evidence: most of the volume growth is flowing to the models that charge the least

theme_stances.key_argument: Revenue sustainability without the capex anchor is the missing link, and vendor financing blurs revenue and financing lines.
theme_stances.evidence: The missing link here is sustainability and the ability for those revenues to persist
